claims.text: Sustained high-temperature oxidation resistance and material integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys are primarily governed by formation of a continuous, adherent, slow-growing protective oxide scale.
Aluminum- and chromium-enriched oxide scales can act as diffusion barriers to oxygen ingress.
The proposed baseline is an equiatomic multiprincipal-element alloy produced by melting and homogenization and containing nominal Al and Cr.
The controlled intervention is to increase the relative Al and Cr contents while keeping the other principal elements constant.
The baseline and modified alloys will be oxidized in controlled ambient air at approximately 1000°C for 100 hours.
Oxide-scale thickness, continuity, and adhesion govern the rate of oxygen diffusion into the alloy.
At high temperature, protective alloying elements segregate to the surface and preferentially oxidize.
The resulting well-adherent protective oxide scale limits subsequent oxidation by impeding oxygen transport.
Increasing Al and Cr concentrations promotes formation of a more uniform and robust protective oxide layer.
A more uniform and robust protective layer mitigates oxygen diffusion and oxidation-induced degradation.
Relative to the baseline, alloys with increased Al and Cr will exhibit lower oxidation weight gain.
Relative to the baseline, alloys with increased Al and Cr will form thinner and more continuous oxide scales.
Relative to the baseline, alloys with increased Al and Cr will better maintain material integrity during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The baseline alloy is expected to form a less uniform or more defective scale and consequently oxidize faster.
The proposed behavior is expected to apply from approximately 800°C to 1100°C when oxidation kinetics are diffusion controlled and the alloys remain phase stable.
Formation of non-protective brittle oxides or high-temperature phase destabilization may invalidate the proposed behavior.
The critical Al and Cr concentrations needed to reliably form a protective scale are unknown.
Possible interactions between Al or Cr and the other alloying elements are unknown.
Weight gain, scale morphology and thickness, scale chemistry, and oxide phases can be evaluated using gravimetry, SEM, EDS, and XRD.
Failure of the higher-Al/Cr alloy to reduce weight gain or improve scale continuity and adherence, or appearance of detrimental phases, would falsify the proposed beneficial-barrier mechanism.
